title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #89** is the famous distinct distances problem, posed in 1946.

**The Question**: Does every set of n points in ℝ² determine at least Ω(n/√(log n)) distinct distances?

**Status**: OPEN (original conjecture)

**Partial Result**: Guth-Katz (2015) proved Ω(n/log n)

**Prize**: $500
mathContext: This is one of Erdős's most celebrated problems in combinatorial geometry. The √n × √n integer grid achieves O(n/√(log n)) distances, showing the conjecture would be tight.

title: The Distinct Distances Problem
content:
Given n points in the plane, how many distinct pairwise distances must exist?

The **√n × √n integer grid** is the key extremal example. Points of the form (i, j) for 0 ≤ i, j < √n have distances determined by sums of two squares.

A classical result in number theory shows such grids have only O(n/√(log n)) distinct distances.
mathContext: The number of integers ≤ x representable as sums of two squares is ~cx/√(log x). This controls the grid's distinct distances.

title: Distinct Distances
content:
**dist p q** is the Euclidean distance ‖p - q‖ between points.

**distinctDistances S** is the set of all positive pairwise distances in S.

We use `S.offDiag` to get pairs (p, q) with p ≠ q, then image the distance function and filter out zero.
mathContext: Formally: `(S.offDiag.image fun pq => dist pq.1 pq.2).filter (· > 0)`

title: Minimum Distinct Distances g(n)
content:
**minDistinctDistances n** is g(n), the minimum number of distinct distances over all n-point sets in ℝ².

This is THE extremal function that Erdős asked about: what is g(n) asymptotically?
mathContext: Defined as `sInf {numDistinctDistances S | S.card = n}` over all n-point sets S.

title: The Main Conjecture (OPEN)
content:
**Erdos89Conjecture** states: g(n) ≥ c·n/√(log n) for some c > 0 and all large n.

Formally: ∃ c > 0 such that eventually c·n/√(log n) ≤ g(n).

This would be tight by the grid construction.
mathContext: The bound Ω(n/√(log n)) is the conjectured answer. The grid shows O(n/√(log n)) is achievable.

title: Guth-Katz Theorem (2015)
content:
The **Guth-Katz Theorem** is the breakthrough result: g(n) ≥ c·n/log n for some c > 0.

This is weaker than the conjecture by a factor of √(log n), but was a major breakthrough after decades of work.

This result is described in a comment block, not formalized as a Lean axiom or theorem — the proof uses sophisticated algebraic geometry techniques (polynomial partitioning) outside the scope of this file.
mathContext: Guth and Katz proved this using a polynomial method, counting incidences between points and lines in 3D.

title: Grid Upper Bound
content:
The **grid upper bound** states: g(n) ≤ c·n/√(log n) for some c > 0.

The √n × √n integer grid achieves this bound, showing the conjecture is tight if true.

This is described in a comment block, not formalized as a Lean axiom or theorem — the argument uses number theory: the count of integers ≤ x representable as sums of two squares.
mathContext: The Landau-Ramanujan constant governs this: |{n ≤ x : n = a² + b²}| ~ Kx/√(log x).

title: Conjecture Implies Guth-Katz
content:
**conjecture_implies_guthKatz** shows the conjecture is strictly stronger than Guth-Katz.

The key: n/√(log n) > n/log n for large n, since √(log n) < log n.

This is a genuine Lean theorem, fully proved (0 sorries).
mathContext: The proof uses `filter_upwards` to work with the eventually filter and `calc` for the chain of inequalities.

title: Historical Development
content:
The problem saw steady progress over decades:

- **1992**: Chung proves Ω(n^(4/5))
- **2001**: Solymosi-Tóth prove Ω(n^(6/7))
- **2004**: Tardos proves Ω(n^0.8641)
- **2015**: Guth-Katz prove Ω(n/log n)

These historical bounds are described in prose only; they are not formalized as Lean declarations (no `chung1992` or `tardos2004` axioms or theorems exist in this file).
mathContext: The exponent improved from 0.8 to 0.86 to... finally escaping polynomial bounds in 2015.

title: Single Point Conjecture
content:
**singlePointConjecture** (Problem #604) is a stronger version: there's always a SINGLE point determining Ω(n/√(log n)) distances.

This would immediately imply Problem #89, since the total distinct distances includes those from any single point.
mathContext: This asks for a 'rich' point that sees many distances, not just that the whole set has many.
